steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Eye contact
steps.description:
Write down a prediction: “If I say hello first and don't hide my eyes, what will happen is…”

Why: a greeting is the shortest, safest way to start contact first. It's an easy place to begin getting used to it.

Important: this program does not replace therapy. If anxiety gets in the way of your life or you have panic attacks, please talk to a professional.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: The goal is not to never look away. The goal is to stop hiding automatically.
steps.quoteNote: Looking away is normal; the only problem is the automatic escape. Today notice the moment you want to hide and hold on one second longer.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Eye contact
steps.description:
Be the first to greet three people at a suitable moment. Keep eye contact at a level that's comfortable for you, without turning it into a contest. The other person doesn't have to respond.

Easier: Greet one acquaintance first.
Harder (optional): Greet three people first, including someone you barely know.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you greeted your chosen number of people first. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Voice
steps.description:
Read any paragraph aloud a little louder and slower than usual. Listen to yourself once, without criticism.

Why: quiet, rushed speech often keeps anxiety going. A full sentence at your own pace shows you that people hear you without apologies.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: A confident voice isn't a loud voice. It's speech that doesn't ask permission to speak.
steps.quoteNote: Confidence sounds like finishing your sentence and not apologizing for it. Test that today in one request.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Calm voice
steps.description:
Place one order or make one request in a full sentence, at a comfortable pace. You don't need to make your voice deeper or louder. Pauses and a shaky voice are fine.

Easier: Ask someone you know one short question in a full sentence.
Harder (optional): Ask in person a question you usually put off.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you made one clear request. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Direct speech without downplaying
steps.description:
Recall phrases you habitually use to shrink your words, for example: “This is probably a stupid question, but…”, “I'm not sure, but maybe…”, “Sorry to bother you…”, “It's nothing, really…”. Prepare a direct replacement. Tell habitual downplaying apart from appropriate politeness and honest doubt.

Why: these phrases ask the listener in advance not to take you seriously. Dropping them tests that direct words don't lead to disaster.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Politeness doesn't require lowering the value of your words in advance.
steps.quoteNote: You can be gentle without discounting what you say. Today keep the politeness but drop the “this is probably silly” disclaimer.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Direct speech without downplaying
steps.description:
In three situations of your choice, drop the habitual downplaying of your words and say it directly. Keep appropriate politeness, an honest “I don't know” and apologies for real mistakes.

Easier: Drop the habitual downplaying once.
Harder (optional): Do it in a conversation that matters to you.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you made your chosen number of conscious replacements. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Preference out loud
steps.description:
Write down a prediction: “If I say directly what I want, people will…”

Why: when you stay silent about what you want, others decide for you. Small preferences are a safe way to practice your right to want things.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Having a preference doesn't make you difficult. It gives others clear information about you.
steps.quoteNote: Saying “I'd like…” helps others rather than imposing on them. Today see how people react to a clear preference.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Say what you want
steps.description:
State a real preference three times. At least once, suggest an option yourself without waiting to be asked.

Easier: State one genuine preference to someone you know.
Harder (optional): Suggest an option to a small group yourself.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you stated your chosen number of genuine preferences. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Your own pace
steps.description:
Recall conversations where you rush to answer. Decide in advance: today I answer at my own pace.

Why: rushing to answer is a common way to escape awkwardness quickly. A pause shows you that silence is bearable and people will wait.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: A pause before answering isn't weakness. You have the right to think first.
steps.quoteNote: A short silence feels long only to you. Today let yourself think and notice whether the other person waits.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: The right to pause
steps.description:
At least three times, when a question needs thought, think first and only then answer. Don't apologize for a natural pause.

Easier: Once, give yourself time to think before answering.
Harder (optional): In an important conversation, say: “I need to think about it, I'll get back to you by…” and name a time.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you gave yourself time to think in the chosen situation. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Asking a stranger
steps.description:
Write down a prediction: “If I approach a stranger, they will…”

Why: asking a stranger something practical is a clear reason to speak, and that kind of conversation has a natural end.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: First contact can be awkward. You don't have to wait for full confidence to try.
steps.quoteNote: The awkwardness of first contact is a normal part of the skill, not a sign you're doing it wrong. Today start without waiting for the fear to go away.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Speak up first
steps.description:
Ask two strangers a real factual question at a suitable moment. Don't invent unnecessary questions just for the count. If the person is busy or doesn't want to talk, wrap up.

Easier: Ask a staff member one question you actually need, within their job.
Harder (optional): Ask a real question to a stranger who isn't busy.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you made your chosen number of appropriate approaches, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Repeat at your own pace
steps.description:
Pick a useful exercise from this week that you want to consolidate. Decide which version is doable right now: easier, the same or a bit harder.

Why: skills stick through repetition. Repeating a familiar step shows that your anxiety around it is already lower.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Growth becomes visible when the same action needs less avoidance, or when you can make it harder.
steps.quoteNote: Progress isn't only new tasks; it's also earlier ones getting easier. Compare today's anxiety rating with your first attempt.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Repeat at your own pace
steps.description:
Pick a useful exercise from this week and repeat it. Keep the difficulty or ease it if you need to. Making it harder is optional; after a missed day you can simply continue.

Easier: Repeat the chosen action in an easier version.
Harder (optional): Make just one element harder: the context or the number of repetitions.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you repeated the chosen action at a doable level. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Start and open up
steps.description:
Prepare two open questions: not “How are you?”, but a question people want to answer in detail.

Why: conversations run on reciprocity: when you share something about yourself, it's easier for the other person to do the same.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Initiative starts before you feel fully ready.
steps.quoteNote: If you wait until it's not scary at all, the conversation may never start. Today begin with a prepared question even if you're nervous.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Start a conversation
steps.description:
Start a conversation yourself with an acquaintance or colleague and share something about yourself. If the interest is mutual, keep it going for a few exchanges. Pauses are fine; if the other person is busy, wrap up.

Easier: Start a short conversation with an acquaintance and share one fact about yourself.
Harder (optional): Start a conversation with a colleague you barely know and share your impression of something.
Online option: Message someone you haven't talked to in a while, ask one of your prepared questions and share something about yourself.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you started a conversation and offered a topic or shared something about yourself; continuing is optional. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Suggest first
steps.description:
Formulate one real suggestion in advance, in one sentence.

Why: suggesting first means influencing what happens, not just adapting to it.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Your suggestion can be turned down and still be a perfectly normal suggestion.
steps.quoteNote: Turning down a suggestion is a response to the idea, not to you. Today make a suggestion and notice that people simply discuss it.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Make the first suggestion
steps.description:
When there's a choice to make, be the first to suggest your option. If there's no such situation, create one naturally: suggest a plan, place, time or next step.

Easier: Suggest one small next step to someone you know.
Harder (optional): Suggest a concrete plan to a group and listen to objections.
Online option: In a group chat, be the first to suggest an option: a time, a place or a next step.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you made one real suggestion. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: A request that might get a “no”
steps.description:
Write down the answer you expect and finish the sentence: “If I'm turned down, what I'll actually lose is…”

Why: the fear of rejection is often stronger than the rejection itself. A small real request tests that prediction in practice.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: A request succeeds when you asked clearly, not when the other person agreed.
steps.quoteNote: You're responsible for a clear request; the answer is the other person's choice. Today give yourself credit just for asking.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: A real request
steps.description:
Make a small real request to someone who is free to say no. The request should be something you actually need, not invented for the exercise.

Easier: Ask someone you know for a small real favor.
Harder (optional): Make such a request to someone you barely know, in a suitable situation.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you made a real request, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: A line to a stranger
steps.description:
Pick a natural situation with people around: a queue, public transport, a shop, a class. Prepare one fitting line about the situation and write down your prediction of the reaction.

Why: after practical questions, the next step is a line with no practical need behind it. It trains your right to simply speak up.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Starting a conversation is your part. Whether the other person wants to continue is theirs.
steps.quoteNote: Your task is to start respectfully; how it continues depends on both of you. Today judge yourself by the first line, not by the length of the conversation.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Speak to a stranger
steps.description:
Say one fitting line about the situation to a stranger: a short comment, a question or a thank-you. You don't have to keep talking; if the person is busy or closed off, wrap up calmly.

Easier: Say one line more than usual to someone who is there for work: a cashier, a barista, a driver.
Harder (optional): Start a conversation with a stranger and keep it going for a few exchanges if the interest is mutual.
Online option: Post a thoughtful comment or question in a topic-based chat or community and reply if someone responds.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you respectfully said your chosen line, regardless of the response. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: A specific invitation
steps.description:
Choose a person and a specific format for meeting. Write down what a possible “no” would mean to you.

Why: an invitation is a step from casual contact toward a relationship. The risk of hearing “no” is noticeable here, but the consequences are usually small.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: A declined invitation tells you the person's answer; it doesn't define your worth.
steps.quoteNote: A “no” can mean “busy”, “not now” or “not my thing”, and none of these says anything about your worth. Today keep the answer separate from your self-esteem.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Invite specifically
steps.description:
Invite a specific person to a specific activity and suggest a time or period: a walk, coffee, sports, a movie. Leave them free to decline or not answer; don't push for a yes with repeated asks.

Easier: Send an acquaintance a specific invitation in writing.
Harder (optional): Invite someone in person; if there's mutual interest, it can be a date.
Online option: Invite an acquaintance to a call, an online game or a watch party at a specific time.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you sent or said a specific invitation, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Initiative in a decision
steps.description:
Find a small situation with two or more people where you can suggest a concrete next step.

Why: suggesting a solution to a group is harder than to one person: the attention of several people is the next level.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Initiative means suggesting a direction, not taking away others' right to object.
steps.quoteNote: Taking the initiative isn't bossing people around: you set a direction and others can adjust it. Today make a suggestion and leave room for objections.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Take the initiative
steps.description:
In a situation with two or more people, suggest a concrete solution: a route, a place, a next step or how to split a small task. Leave room for objections.

Easier: Suggest a next step on a shared task to one person.
Harder (optional): Suggest a plan to a small group and take on one agreed task yourself.
Online option: In a family, friends' or work chat, suggest a concrete plan: a time, a place or who does what.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you suggested a solution and named your possible next step; the group doesn't have to agree. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Double initiative
steps.description:
Pick two natural situations: one for a conversation and one for a suggestion or invitation.

Why: doing the same action in different situations makes the skill stable instead of tied to one place.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: A skill sticks not through understanding but through repetition in different situations.
steps.quoteNote: Understanding a skill isn't the same as having it. Today repeat what you've learned in two different situations.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Two actions
steps.description:
During the day, start one conversation yourself and make one suggestion or invitation.

Easier: Choose one of the two actions.
Harder (optional): Do both actions in different settings, for example at work and with friends.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you completed the option you chose in advance: one or both actions. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: “No” without excuses
steps.description:
Prepare a calm phrase: “No, that doesn't work for me” or “Thanks, I'm fine.”

Why: being able to say no protects your time and energy. A short refusal without long excuses shows that relationships usually survive it.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: “No” can be respectful and enough.
steps.quoteNote: Long excuses often soothe your own guilt rather than the other person. Today try a short, polite no.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Say “no”
steps.description:
Turn down one real offer or request that doesn't suit you. A short explanation is fine; a long defensive speech isn't needed.

Easier: Turn down a small optional offer, for example an upsell in a shop: “Thanks, I'm fine.”
Harder (optional): Turn down extra workload and, if you like, suggest a suitable alternative.

If there's no situation for a refusal today: prepare the phrase and use it at the next opportunity.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you expressed a real refusal in the chosen situation; if there was no situation, when your phrase is ready and you've picked where to use it. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Disagreeing on substance
steps.description:
Prepare the formula: “I see it differently, because…” plus one argument.

Why: agreeing just to keep the peace builds up resentment. Calm disagreement shows that different opinions don't destroy contact.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Confidence doesn't require always being right. It lets you take part honestly in disagreement.
steps.quoteNote: You don't need to be 100% sure to speak up. Today say how you see it and be ready to hear the arguments.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Disagree calmly
steps.description:
In a real conversation, express genuine disagreement and explain your position with one argument. Don't give up your position just to ease tension; accepting a good argument is fine.

Easier: Express genuine disagreement on a small issue to someone you know.
Harder (optional): Explain your position in a work discussion while staying open to arguments.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you voiced genuine disagreement and explained it; changing your mind after hearing arguments is fine. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Ask for support
steps.description:
Choose someone you trust. Name a difficulty you're ready to share and the support you need. Prepare a phrase: “I'm having a hard time with… Could you…?”

Why: the habit of carrying everything alone increases isolation. Asking for support is also a confidence skill, not a weakness.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: You can ask for support even if you're used to coping on your own.
steps.quoteNote: Independence is valuable, but it doesn't forbid leaning on others. Today let yourself ask.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Ask for support
steps.description:
Tell someone you trust about one real difficulty and ask for specific support: to listen, to be there or to help with a small task. First check whether now is a good time for them. You decide what to share.

Easier: Ask someone close to give you a few minutes at a convenient time.
Harder (optional): Tell them about the difficulty in person and name the support you need without downplaying it.

If there's no one to ask: reach out to an interest group or support group, a helpline or a professional. That is asking for support too.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you asked for specific support, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Boundary
steps.description:
Choose a real boundary that has bothered you for a while: time, workload, communication style or personal space. Write down your wording. For example: “I can help until 7 pm; after that I'm offline” or “It matters to me to finish my thought, please don't interrupt.”

Why: until you voice your boundaries, others don't know something bothers you. One calm sentence about a boundary often solves what has been building up for months.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: A boundary describes what you're willing to do and accept. It doesn't have to punish anyone.
steps.quoteNote: A boundary is information about you, not a reproach. Today state it calmly, without blame.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: State a boundary
steps.description:
Calmly state an existing boundary to the person it concerns. If they push against it, calmly repeat your position once.

Easier: State a small time boundary to someone you know.
Harder (optional): Discuss a recurring workload and name what you're willing to take on.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you clearly stated your chosen boundary; the other person doesn't have to agree. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Handling criticism
steps.description:
Choose a specific piece of work or action where honest feedback would really help you.

Why: fear of being judged keeps many people from acting at all. Feedback you ask for is a safe way to hear criticism in a dose you choose.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Criticism becomes more useful when you can hear it without automatic defense.
steps.quoteNote: When you don't rush to justify yourself, it's easier to find what's useful in criticism. Today listen to the end first and decide later.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Ask for feedback
steps.description:
Ask someone whose opinion you trust what could be improved in a specific piece of work or action. If you get an answer, listen, clarify if needed and decide for yourself what to use. You can take a pause; you don't have to agree with everything.

Easier: Send one specific feedback question to someone you trust.
Harder (optional): Ask for feedback in person and, if you get an answer, ask for one example.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you asked a specific feedback question; no answer doesn't cancel it. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Raising a problem
steps.description:
Prepare a sentence using the pattern fact → effect → request. No accusations or labels. Example: “The dishes have been in the sink for three days (fact). It makes cooking hard for me (effect). Let's agree to wash them by the evening (request).”

Why: problems nobody talks about usually grow. The fact → effect → request pattern helps you speak directly without attacking.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Raising a problem directly is often kinder than letting irritation build up.
steps.quoteNote: Silence feels considerate, but irritation leaks out anyway. Today raise the problem calmly while it's still small.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Raise a problem
steps.description:
Discuss one real small problem directly with the person it concerns, using fact → effect → request.

Easier: Discuss a small household problem with someone you know.
Harder (optional): Raise a recurring work problem and suggest a specific change.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you named the fact, its effect and your request, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Holding your position
steps.description:
Recall a real difference of opinion that you usually keep quiet about.

Why: keeping your opinion under pressure is the next step after simple disagreement.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Someone else's disagreement is unpleasant, but it doesn't make your position wrong by itself.
steps.quoteNote: An objection is another point of view, not proof that you're wrong. Today listen and decide yourself whether to change your position.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Stand by your view
steps.description:
Share your real opinion when it differs from another person's or a group's. Don't invent an argument. Pause before responding to objections: you can keep your view or change it if the arguments convinced you.

Easier: Share a differing opinion in a one-on-one conversation.
Harder (optional): Share it in a small group and listen to the other side.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you honestly stated your position; you don't need to win the argument or hide your nerves. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Postponed conversation #1
steps.description:
Make a list of three conversations or actions you've been putting off because of awkwardness or fear of the reaction. Pick the most moderate and safe one.

Why: avoidance keeps anxiety going: the longer you put something off, the scarier it gets. One postponed conversation often relieves more tension than a week of thinking.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Avoidance often makes a short conversation heavier in your head than it turns out in reality.
steps.quoteNote: In your head, a conversation picks up worst-case scenarios. Today check how hard it really is.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Do what you've postponed
steps.description:
Have the chosen safe conversation today: ask a long-standing question, clear up something left unsaid, state expectations or apologize if you've been meaning to.

Easier: Start with a short message on the substance of the postponed issue.
Harder (optional): Have the conversation in person if it's appropriate and safe.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you started discussing the chosen issue on substance; if the person is unavailable, a meaningful message counts. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Word and deed
steps.description:
Choose a small task of 5–20 minutes whose result depends on you. Decide whom you'll tell about it: a friend, a colleague or a group chat. Write down: what I'll do, by when and how I'll know it's done.

Why: saying your plan out loud and keeping your word builds trust in yourself (self-efficacy) and gets you used to others seeing your commitments.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Self-trust grows when what you said out loud becomes what you did.
steps.quoteNote: When others know about your promise, keeping it strengthens confidence even more. Today promise a little and keep your word.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Promise and deliver
steps.description:
Tell one person what small task you'll do today and by what time. Do it and briefly let them know it's done. Don't add new requirements along the way.

Easier: Share your plan in a message and, once it's done, reply with one word: “Done.”
Harder (optional): Share the plan in person or in a group and briefly tell them about the result afterward.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you stated your promise, completed the chosen step and reported the result. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Being visible
steps.description:
Write down a prediction: “If I draw attention to myself with a meaningful action, people will think…”

Why: staying in the shadows protects you from judgment but costs you influence. One meaningful visible action shows that attention is bearable.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Being noticed for your contribution is a normal part of taking part, not a demand to be liked by everyone.
steps.quoteNote: Being visible doesn't mean everyone has to like you. Today show up with substance and don't measure the result by approval.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Be visible for your contribution
steps.description:
Do one meaningful action that makes you more visible: ask a question at a meeting, suggest an idea to a group or share your own reasoned position.

Easier: Ask one meaningful question in a small group you know.
Harder (optional): Briefly present your idea at a meeting or publish a reasoned position.
Online option: Ask a question or share your opinion in a topic community or under a post on your subject.

Safety: if you post your opinion online, choose a topic you're safe discussing publicly, don't reveal personal data and remember that people beyond your acquaintances may see it.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you did one meaningful action, regardless of attention or approval. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Not shrinking next to authority
steps.description:
Choose a person around whom you automatically feel less important or competent. Prepare a sincere question.

Why: anxiety rises most next to people who seem higher in status. Talking as equals shows that your opinion carries weight too.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Someone else's authority doesn't require you to shrink next to them.
steps.quoteNote: Respecting someone and not making yourself smaller are fully compatible. Today talk to them as one adult to another.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: A conversation without shrinking
steps.description:
Start a normal, meaningful conversation yourself with someone next to whom you usually shrink. The goal isn't to prove status but to talk as equals.

Easier: Send one specific question to someone you respect.
Harder (optional): Start the conversation in person and add your own suggestion on the topic.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you started meaningful contact or sent a specific question, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Allowing yourself to be a beginner
steps.description:
Finish the sentence: “If others see that I don't know or can't do something, then…”

Why: fear of looking incompetent gets in the way of learning. An open “I don't know” usually draws less judgment than you expect.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Not knowing is the normal state before knowing.
steps.quoteNote: Everyone who can do something once couldn't. Today show that you don't know and see how people react.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Show that you're learning
steps.description:
In a safe situation, openly show a lack of knowledge or experience: say “I didn't get that, could you explain again?”, ask a basic question or try a new activity.

Easier: Ask someone you know to explain something you didn't understand.
Harder (optional): Ask a basic question in a group session or try a new skill in front of others.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you openly admitted not knowing and took a step toward learning. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: An important conversation at your own pace
steps.description:
Go back to your list from day 22. Pick a doable, safe topic and write down your first sentence. Repeating the previous level is fine too.

Why: important topics are easier to approach once you already have this month's experience of difficult conversations.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Courage here isn't an irreversible gesture; it's the ability to calmly enter an important conversation.
steps.quoteNote: Courage isn't one bold move but the willingness to calmly start an important conversation. Today take the first step into one.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: An important conversation at your own pace
steps.description:
Choose an important, safe conversation from your day 22 list. You can repeat the previous level; making it harder is optional. State your thought and request without ultimatums. If the other person is unavailable, write on substance or choose another doable topic.

Easier: Discuss one small point of the chosen topic or repeat a day 22 level conversation.
Harder (optional): Discuss a more significant topic without ultimatums or demands for an immediate decision.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you said or wrote something substantive on the chosen topic; the other person's decision isn't part of the criterion. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Full cycle
steps.description:
Choose a situation that combines your initiative, your position, a specific request and the possibility of refusal. Write down your prediction.

Why: in real life, skills rarely show up one at a time. Here you combine initiative, position and request in one action.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Confidence shows especially where you act without control over the other person's answer.
steps.quoteNote: You don't control the other person's answer, but you do control how clearly you speak. Test that today with a real proposal.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Act without guarantees
steps.description:
Propose a real idea or change to someone who may disagree. Give your reasons and ask for a specific next step, decision or time to reply.

Easier: Propose a small change to someone you know and ask for a specific next step.
Harder (optional): Discuss a significant work or shared proposal and the possible responses.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you clearly stated your proposal and a specific request, regardless of the answer. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Lock in what's useful
steps.description:
Choose an exercise that matters for your life. Recall your last attempt and decide which version you'll repeat today.

Why: repeating the exercise that's most useful for you turns a one-off act of courage into a habit.
steps.tip: Before you act, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 and write the number next to your prediction. Repeating or easing a task is fine. Phone notes or a notebook work for writing things down.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: Growth isn't only less anxiety. Sometimes the anxiety stays, but there's less avoidance.
steps.quoteNote: The goal isn't to stop feeling nervous but to let nerves decide less for you. Compare your anxiety rating with your first attempt.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Lock in what's useful
steps.description:
Choose an exercise from this month that matters to you and repeat it at a doable level. You don't have to pick the most unpleasant one or make it harder. Compare what you did now and before, even if the nerves are still there.

Easier: Repeat the chosen exercise in an easier version.
Harder (optional): Change one element of the task if the usual version already feels doable.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you repeated the chosen action at a suitable level. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 again. What did you expect, and what actually happened? What did you do to make it less scary (holding your phone, prepared lines, looking away)? Could you skip one of those next time?

steps.title: Preparation
steps.subtitle: Review and next steps
steps.description:
Reread your notes from the month. Find a case where a bad prediction didn't come true and, if there was one, a refusal or awkward moment you handled. Compare your before and after anxiety ratings at the start and end of the month. If you didn't keep notes, recall one specific example from memory.

Why: a review helps you see real changes and plan practice after the program so the skill doesn't fade.
steps.tip: Before the review, rate your anxiety from 0 to 10 at the thought of starting a conversation with a stranger and compare it with your numbers from the first days. Concrete observations are enough. If something is still hard, that's a direction for practice, not a verdict on your worth.

steps.title: Thought of the day
steps.description: Read this thought before the main task.
steps.quoteText: The goal of the month isn't to become someone without doubts, but to let doubts choose for you less often.
steps.quoteNote: Doubts may remain; what matters is that they stop you less often. Today note where you acted despite doubts.

steps.title: Main challenge
steps.subtitle: Review and next steps
steps.description:
Sum it up: write down three specific actions you can now do and what you still want to practice. Choose one to repeat next week and set a date. You can reuse completed tasks at your own pace.

Easier: Choose one useful action to repeat and set a date.
Harder (optional): Plan three doable steps of different difficulty and set a date for the first.
steps.tip:
Pick one option; the easier one counts too. Done when you wrote your summary and set a date for your next practice; for the easier option, one action and a date are enough. Nerves and imperfect words are fine.

After: what changed this month in how you act when you're anxious? What will help you keep going without the program?
